title: NashDreamer: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
claim: A centralized model unrolled on joint actions and observations, plus per-player infoset models, trains on real trajectories step by step.
layout: 2 time-step columns, top-to-bottom flow, curved skip arrows, legend top-right
description: The figure shows two time steps (t=1 and t=2) side by side. Each column starts at the top with a green box of real data containing observations, reward, done flag and actions. Orange (Player 1) and teal (Player 2) infoset boxes sit below, linked across time by horizontal arrows. Dashed red arrows labeled Unifier Loss run from the infoset boxes into the blue deterministic latent h in a gray dashed Central WM box. Below h, a dashed arrow leads to a posterior stochastic latent z drawn as a small black-and-white grid. Long black curved arrows carry joint actions and observations from the real data into the central model. An arrow from z feeds the next h. Each column ends in a Predictions box. A legend at top right explains the colors.
caption: Two steps of NashDreamer world-model training on a real trajectory. The centralized RSSM is unrolled on the joint action and joint observation, the infoset model separately for each player. All stochastic states are posterior. The KL losses are omitted; ad is the initial dummy action.
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has achieved remarkable results in single-agent domains, yet its extension to competitive imperfect information games (IIGs) remains underexplored. In multi-agent settings, opponent-induced non-stationarity complicates the learning process, and decentralized model learning faces severe identifiability barriers, which we argue make centralized model learning a mathematical necessity. Building on this analysis, we propose NashDreamer, a principled MBRL framework for two-player zero-sum IIGs. It introduces a centralized Multi-Agent Recurrent State-Space Model (MARSSM) that decouples environment dynamics from the effect of players' strategies on their individual observations. NashDreamer is designed to use arbitrary policy gradient algorithms and inherits their convergence guarantees towards Nash equilibria under an idealized model. Empirical evaluations across five benchmark games demonstrate that NashDreamer substantially improves sample efficiency over model-free baselines early in the training. Finally, we theoretically analyze the architecture's optimization landscape, identifying the vulnerability of the Dreamer family of algorithms to posterior collapse in stochastic environments. We leave it as an open challenge.
